candidate_sources.title: Cercospora longipes (brown leaf spot of sugarcane) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Datasheet on Cercospora longipes covering Identity, Distribution, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, and Further Information. C. longipes has a restricted host range: only Saccharum officinarum, S. spontaneum, S. robustum and Sorghum vulgare were infected. Water helps dislodge conidia; incidence highest after rainy seasons. Optimal growth at 25°C, spore germination favored by light and high humidity above 95%.

candidate_sources.title: Cooperative Extension - Agriculture - Sugarcane Diseases
candidate_sources.snippet: Palm Beach County Cooperative Extension page covering sugarcane diseases in Florida including brown spot, brown rust, and other foliar diseases. Describes symptoms as small elongated yellowish spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces that increase in size and turn brown to orange-brown.

candidate_sources.title: Brown spot disease of sugarcane caused by Cercospora longipes (Butler) | RUFORUM Institutional Repository
candidate_sources.snippet: Research document on brown spot disease of sugarcane caused by Cercospora longipes Butler. Results from disease resistance trials indicated a range of reactions from tolerant varieties to highly susceptible cultivators, with no variety found immune to brown spot disease. Spores tolerate desiccation for periods longer than 96 hours and the pathogen is carried over seasons on cane leaf trash.

candidate_sources.title: SUGARCANE :: MAJOR DISEASE :: GRASSY SHOOT
candidate_sources.snippet: Grassy shoot disease of sugarcane caused by phytoplasma (Candidatus Phytoplasma sacchari). Symptoms include proliferation of tillers giving a grassy appearance, white or creamy yellow chlorotic leaves, stunted canes with reduced internodal length, and axillary bud sprouting. Transmitted via infected setts and leafhopper vectors. University agricultural extension lecture covering symptoms, pathogen, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Grassy Shoot of Sugarcane | Pests & Diseases
candidate_sources.snippet: Dedicated page on grassy shoot disease of sugarcane caused by Candidatus Phytoplasma sacchari. Covers symptoms (profuse tillering, white papery leaves, no cane formation), biological triggers (phytoplasma transmitted by leafhoppers and infected setts), and organic and chemical management measures.

candidate_sources.title: Grassy Shoot Management in Sugarcane: Disease Symptoms, Identification, Treatment, Chemical, Biological, Natural, and Organic Control
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive guide on sugarcane grassy shoot disease management. Covers symptoms (chlorotic tillers, white leaf veins, no cane formation), pathogen identification (Ca. Phytoplasma sacchari, 16SrXI group), transmission by leafhoppers (Deltocephalus vulgaris, Exitianus indicus), and control methods including resistant varieties, roguing, moist hot air treatment of setts at 50°C, and avoiding ratooning when GSD incidence exceeds 15%.

candidate_sources.title: SS-AGR-201/SC001: Sugarcane Leaf Scald
candidate_sources.snippet: UF/IFAS Extension factsheet on sugarcane leaf scald caused by Xanthomonas albilineans. Covers symptoms including white pencil lines on leaves, leaf necrosis, scalded appearance, and latent infections. Discusses pathogen biology, transmission via infected setts and cutting tools, and management through resistant varieties and sanitation.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Diseases: Gummosis and Leaf Scald | Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service
candidate_sources.snippet: USDA APHIS page covering sugarcane leaf scald and gummosis. Describes leaf scald caused by Xanthomonas albilineans with symptoms of white pencil-like lines, chlorosis, inward curling of leaves, and sudden plant death in acute phase. Recommends using resistant plants, disease-free cuttings, removing susceptible plant parts, and sanitation of cutting equipment.

candidate_sources.title: Recent Advances in Sugarcane Leaf Scald Disease: Pathogenic Insights and Sustainable Management Approaches
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive 2024 peer-reviewed review of sugarcane leaf scald disease caused by Xanthomonas albilineans. Covers pathogenesis, chronic and acute symptom phases, white pencil lines, leaf chlorosis, albinism in lateral buds, vascular reddish discoloration, yield losses exceeding 40%, juice quality reduction of 30%, and sustainable management including silicon plus bactericide treatments.

candidate_sources.title: Pokkah Boeng - Disease of Sugarcane (TNAU Agritech Portal)
candidate_sources.snippet: Dedicated page on Pokkah Boeng disease of sugarcane from Tamil Nadu Agricultural University. Covers symptoms (chlorotic patches on young leaves, malformation, knife-cut lesions on stalks, top rot), causal organism (Fusarium moniliforme / Fusarium verticillioides), and management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Pokkah Boeng | Pests & Diseases - Plantix
candidate_sources.snippet: Detailed disease profile for Pokkah Boeng of sugarcane. Describes symptoms including chlorotic patches, leaf malformation, twisted spindle, knife-cut wounds on stalks, and top rot in severe cases. Lists Fusarium moniliforme as causal agent. Includes management options: resistant varieties, removing infected tops, fungicide sprays (carbendazim, copper oxychloride, mancozeb).

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Pokkah Boeng Disease: Insights and Future Directions for Effective Management
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive peer-reviewed review (2024) covering Pokkah Boeng disease. Discusses the Fusarium species complex (F. sacchari, F. verticillioides, F. proliferatum, F. andiyazi, F. incarnatum) as causal agents. Details symptom stages (chlorotic phase, acute/knife-cut phase, top rot phase), epidemiology (airborne spread, hot humid conditions), yield losses (10-38%), and integrated management strategies including resistant varieties, biocontrol, and fungicides.

candidate_sources.title: SUGARCANE :: MAJOR DISEASE :: SETT ROT OR PINEAPPLE DISEASE
candidate_sources.snippet: The affected tissues first develop a reddish colour which turns to brownish black in the later stages. The severely affected setts show internodal cavities covered with the mycelium and abundant spores, and a characteristic pineapple smell is associated with the rotting tissues. Caused by Ceratocystis paradoxa (Thielaviopsis paradoxa).

candidate_sources.title: Ceratocystis paradoxa (black rot of pineapple) - CABI PlantWise Plus
candidate_sources.snippet: Ceratocystis paradoxa causes pineapple disease in sugarcane. Detailed coverage of pathogen biology, host range, geographic distribution, symptoms, and management. Covers sugarcane sett rot, black rot of pineapple, and other hosts.

candidate_sources.title: Surveying Potential Soilborne Pathogens Causing Sett Rot on Sugarcane in Southern Florida | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Survey of soilborne pathogens causing sett rot on sugarcane in southern Florida. Identifies Thielaviopsis spp. and other pathogens associated with sugarcane sett rot. Published in Plant Disease (APS).

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane streak mosaic virus | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on Sugarcane streak mosaic virus (SCSMV), covering identity, distribution, hosts, symptoms, diagnosis, biology and ecology, and management. SCSMV is assigned to genus Poacevirus, family Potyviridae.

candidate_sources.title: Historical Review of Sugarcane Streak Mosaic Virus that Has Recently Emerged in Africa | Phytopathology
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive review of SCSMV (genus Poacevirus, family Potyviridae), first reported in 1932 in Louisiana. Covers symptoms (continuous or discontinuous chlorotic stripes, mosaic and streak patterns on leaves), transmission (mechanical, stem cuttings; no confirmed insect vector, mites suspected), distribution across Asia and recent emergence in Africa, and management (virus-free planting material, resistant varieties).

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Mosaic Disease: Characteristics, Identification and Control
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive review covering mosaic diseases of sugarcane caused by SCMV, SrMV, and SCSMV. Describes symptoms (yellowing, chlorotic streaks, mosaic patterns on new leaves), identification methods, and control strategies including host resistance and sanitation of equipment. Notes that symptoms of SCSMV are similar to those of SCMV and SrMV.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane mosaic virus (sugarcane mosaic) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet covering Impact, Identity, Overview, Associated Diseases, Pests or Pathogens, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Environmental Requirements, Prevention/Control and Further Information for sugarcane mosaic virus.

candidate_sources.title: PP313/PP313: Mosaic Disease of St. Augustinegrass Caused by Sugarcane Mosaic Virus
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Florida IFAS Extension factsheet on mosaic disease caused by Sugarcane mosaic virus. Covers symptoms (blotchy or streaky patterns of yellow and green color, broken yellow streaks between veins), transmission by aphids and mechanical means, pathogen biology (family Potyviridae), and management through host resistance.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Mosaic Disease: Characteristics, Identification and Control
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive peer-reviewed review covering sugarcane mosaic disease caused by SCMV, SrMV, and SCSMV. Discusses symptoms (chlorotic or yellowish stripes alternating with normal green on younger foliage, yellow stripes on leaf sheath and stalks, elongated necrotic lesions, stem splitting, stunting), aphid transmission, and control through resistant varieties and sanitation.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Disease | EDIS (UF/IFAS Extension)
candidate_sources.snippet: SS-AGR-256: Initial symptoms include yellowing of the lower surface of the leaf midrib on leaves 3 to 6 counting from the top expanding spindle leaf. Yellowing expands from the midrib into the leaf blade as the season progresses. Caused by Sugarcane yellow leaf virus (SCYLV), transmitted by aphids including Melanaphis sacchari. SCYLV reduces both cane and sugar yield.

candidate_sources.title: Present Status and Future Management Strategies for Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus: A Major Constraint to the Global Sugarcane Production
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive review of SCYLV biology, epidemiology, and management. Symptoms include intense yellowing of midrib extending to leaf blade, tissue necrosis from leaf tip towards base, stunted growth with shortened internodes, and bunchy top appearance. Virus is phloem-limited, transmitted by Melanaphis sacchari in circulative non-propagative manner. Management focuses on resistant varieties and virus-free planting material.

candidate_sources.title: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus – A Silent Threat? | CABI Plant Health Cases
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI case study on ScYLV as a silent threat to sugarcane production. Covers symptom expression, diagnostic approaches, epidemiology, and integrated management strategies. Often asymptomatic, making detection challenging. Discusses global distribution and economic impact.

candidate_sources.title: Mycovellosiella koepkei (yellow spot of sugarcane) | Plantwise Knowledge Bank (CABI)
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet for Mycovellosiella koepkei (Passalora koepkei, Cercospora koepkei), the causal agent of yellow spot disease of sugarcane. Covers distribution, hosts, symptoms, biology, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Plant Pathology Circular No. 289 - Florida Dept. of Agriculture & Consumer Services
candidate_sources.snippet: Yellow spot initially appears as small 1-2mm diameter yellow lesions on leaves, mostly on younger foliage. Lesions enlarge to 1-2cm, irregular and elongated along the leaf axis. Red pigmentation develops around and in lesions as infected leaves mature. Caused by Mycovellosiella koepkei. Fungicides such as benomyl and copper compounds can be used but may be impractical; resistant varieties provide the basis for control.

candidate_sources.title: Identification of a major quantitative trait locus (QTL) for yellow spot (Mycovellosiella koepkei) disease resistance in sugarcane
candidate_sources.snippet: Yellow spot, caused by Mycovellosiella koepkei, is a significant foliar disease of sugarcane. Genetic resistance is common in breeding lines. This study identified a major QTL for yellow spot resistance, providing molecular markers for breeding resistant varieties.
